ECE 6612

XSS and SQL injection

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows untrusted input arriving at a browser interpreter or a database interpreter.

A review page needs to display a customer’s words. A search page needs to place a search value into a database lookup. In both cases an application receives data and chooses how another component will interpret it. Injection happens when attacker-controlled characters gain the structure or execution role reserved for application code.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) runs attacker-controlled code with the vulnerable page’s origin. Stored XSS saves the input in a record, such as a review, that later reaches readers. Reflected XSS returns a value from the current request in an executable context. DOM-based XSS occurs when page JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data and passes it to an unsafe browser sink. A sink is the operation that consumes the data, such as an HTML parser or code evaluator.

Once script runs in the account page’s origin, it can read accessible DOM data and issue actions with that page’s authority. An HttpOnly cookie keeps its value out of JavaScript cookie APIs; browser requests can still attach that cookie. HTTPS protects delivery to the genuine site while the site’s vulnerable content supplies the execution path. The repair belongs at the input-to-interpreter boundary.

Use text-node operations for plain text. When a value belongs in HTML, an attribute, a URL or JavaScript, apply the defense appropriate to that exact context; their parsing rules differ. A well-maintained sanitizer can permit a restricted set of markup where rich content is required. A Content Security Policy (CSP) constrains script and resource execution, such as limiting script-src to approved origins and nonces. Its value depends on which code the policy trusts and whether the execution path is covered.

Structured Query Language (SQL) injection reaches the server’s database query parser. Concatenating an untrusted name into query text can allow punctuation and operators to alter its parse tree. Parentheses, quote context, comment rules and operator precedence determine the resulting query. A database executes the parsed query with the application account’s permissions, so excessive database rights increase possible damage.

A prepared statement sends a fixed SQL structure with placeholders and binds input as parameter values. For SELECT price FROM stock WHERE sku = ?, an arbitrary sku string stays a value for that one placeholder. Dynamic identifiers, such as a selected column name, usually need an explicit allowlist because ordinary value parameters do not stand for query syntax. Least-privilege database accounts limit the resources any successful query can reach. Browser output handling and database parameter binding act at their respective interpreters.

Example

An inventory service binds a user’s product name to a prepared WHERE name = ? query. It then displays the returned name using a DOM text node. Parameter binding keeps the supplied name inside a database value; text insertion keeps the returned characters inside page text. Each defense follows the data into the component that will interpret it.

Sources and scope
  • C16 Web Security: stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS; CSP; SQL parse trees and prepared statements.
  • W3C Content Security Policy: script execution and resource directives.
  • WHATWG HTML: text insertion, parsing and script execution.

Practice

1. A site changes its database lookups to prepared statements. It still displays stored review text by assigning that text to innerHTML. Explain the remaining execution path and a suitable repair.

Name the component that receives the stored text after the database lookup finishes.

A stored review can still reach the browser’s HTML interpreter through innerHTML and create an XSS path. Use textContent for plain reviews, or a carefully maintained markup sanitizer if a restricted rich-text format is required. The prepared query protects the separate database parsing boundary.

2. A site has script-src limited to its own origin, but lets users upload executable JavaScript at that origin. What dependency makes the policy weak?

Follow where the policy’s permitted code can originate.

The policy trusts script served by the site’s origin. User-controlled executable uploads on that origin can supply permitted script, so the allowlist includes attacker-controlled code. Upload handling, content types, execution isolation and the CSP trust set must be designed together.
